top_cited_works.title: Combustion Behavior of Highly Energetic Thermites: Nano versus Micron Composites
top_cited_works.abstract: Combustion behavior of energetic composite materials was experimentally examined for the purpose of evaluating the unique properties of nano-scale compared with traditional micron-scale particulate media. Behavior of composite systems composed of aluminum (Al) and molybdenum trioxide (MoO3) were studied as a function of Al particle size, equivalence ratio and bulk density. Samples were prepared by mechanically mixing individual fuel and oxidizer particles and combustion experiments included measurements of ignition and flame propagation behavior. Ignition was achieved using a 50-W CO2 laser and combustion velocities were measured from photographic data. Reaction kinetics were studied with differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Results indicate that the incorporation of nano-Al particles (1) significantly reduces ignition temperatures and (2) produces unique reaction behavior that can be attributed to a different chemical kinetic mechanism than observed with micron-Al particles.

top_cited_works.title: Combustion velocities and propagation mechanisms of metastable interstitial composites
top_cited_works.abstract: Combustion velocities were experimentally determined for nanocomposite thermite powders composed of aluminum (Al) fuel and molybdenum trioxide (MoO3) oxidizer under well-confined conditions. Pressures were also measured to provide detailed information about the reaction mechanism. Samples of three different fuel particle sizes (44, 80, and 121nm) were analyzed to determine the influence of particle size on combustion velocity. Bulk powder density was varied from approximately 5% to 10% of the theoretical maximum density (TMD). The combustion velocities ranged from approximately 600 to 1000m∕s. Results indicate that combustion velocities increase with decreasing particle size. Pressure measurements indicate that strong convective mechanisms are integral in flame propagation.

recent_works.title: A Computational Approach to the Analysis of the Initial Steps of Dehydration in Aluminum (Oxy)hydroxides
recent_works.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
recent_works.abstract: Modifying the surface chemistry of metal fuels is a strategy to promote greater power generation. Aluminum is a common fuel used in energy generation technologies and is a good candidate to study surface modification. Pyrophoric metals are passivated by their nascent oxide, and for aluminum core particles, the passivation shell is formed by aluminum oxide phases. A hydrated surface modification is a first step toward further transformation into tailored oxygen-rich and stable surface passivation chemistry. Various aluminum hydroxide species are involved in surface modification, of which Al(OH) 3 has been shown to be the most promising. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that removing surface hydroxyls is an endothermic process. In vacuum, boehmite requires ∼365–450 kJ/mol and bayerite ∼216–281 kJ/mol to release water (per site), indicating bayerite is intrinsically easier to dehydroxylate. Implicit solvation (water) reduces these energies by 5–20%, making boehmite and bayerite dehydration energetics more comparable (boehmite: ∼345–390 kJ/mol, bayerite: ∼195–250 kJ/mol for representative sites). recent_works.title: Particle size and oxide shell effects on microwave-induced heating of copper powder compacts
recent_works.venue: Journal of Microwave Power and Electromagnetic Energy
recent_works.abstract: Microwave heating of metallic powders is strongly influenced by particle size, surface oxidation, and electromagnetic coupling, yet the relative contributions of these effects remain incompletely understood. In this study, copper powder compacts with systematically varied particle sizes were exposed to microwave radiation under identical experimental conditions, and the resulting thermal response was monitored using infrared thermography. Smaller particle sizes exhibited significantly enhanced microwave-induced heating compared to larger particles, which increasingly approached bulk-like behaviour. Microstructural and phase characterization revealed size-dependent oxide formation that contributed to differences in thermal response. A simplified heat-transfer model incorporating effective emissivity and convective losses was used to interpret steady-state temperature trends, providing qualitative insight into relative microwave-to-thermal energy conversion across particle sizes. recent_works.title: Controlling Microwave Energy Absorption in Aluminum Particle Compacts by Tuning the Crystallinity of the Alumina Shell
recent_works.abstract: Abstract Microwave-to-thermal energy conversion in aluminum particle compacts can be controlled by modifying the phase and thickness of the native alumina passivation shell. In this study, the alumina shell surrounding aluminum nanoparticles was altered through thermal annealing in air at 400 °C for thermal treatment times of 30, 60, 90, and 120 min. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) revealed shell growth from an average thickness of 2.76 nm to 9.63 nm with increasing annealing time. Thermal treatment also induced a transition from an initially amorphous shell to increasingly crystalline alumina, as confirmed by X-ray Diffraction (XRD). Compacts fabricated from the annealed powders were exposed to microwave radiation at 2.45 GHz for 5 min in an electromagnetic exposure chamber. Transient surface temperatures were recorded in situ using infrared thermograph. Compacts prepared from the as-received powders exhibited significantly higher steady-state temperatures than those made from annealed powders. recent_works.title: Promoting powder suspensions for obscuration by balancing tribocharging and surface energy
recent_works.venue: Journal of Materials Research and Technology
recent_works.abstract: The dynamic relationship between surface energy and tribo-electric charging was studied for optical extinction and emission of aluminum powder suspensions. Particles were dispersed via ballistic impact of loose powder in a visually accessible chamber. Flake particulates were studied, including aluminum (Al) and aluminum surface coated with silica (SiO 2 ) (Al@SiO 2 ). High-speed cameras recorded reactive events in air, and optical extinction events in argon environments. Reactive events generate thermal emission analyzed bi-spectrally (NIR and VIS) and non-reactive events block the transmission of light by reflecting or absorbing a reference backlight; reflection and absorption are not deconvoluted in this study. Al@SiO 2 flakes exhibit broad thermal emission compared to Al in reactive suspensions. Also, the SiO 2 surface coating may delaminate from the Al flake during impact thereby exposing Al and resulting in greater fuel consumption compared to Al flakes. Complex reaction mechanisms between silica, alumina, ambient humidity, and air may contribute to broad thermal emission demonstrated by Al@SiO 2 . recent_works.title: Fundamental calorimetric measurements of boron oxidation from dry powder suspensions
recent_works.abstract: Boron is a promising fuel with exceptional gravimetric and volumetric heat of combustion, yet its full energetic potential remains difficult to realize, particularly when measured in a calorimeter. This study introduces a method to quantify the calorific output of boron powder suspensions by dispersing the powder is a porous carbohydrate (PC) matrix. The PC matrix has a low heat of combustion to provide the organic framework needed to isolate particles and simulate dry powder suspension burning behavior. Bomb calorimetry experiments were performed to measure the available energy of boron powder combustion representative of a dust environment as a function of particle loading density (i.e., called boron loading fraction, BLF).
